pages.text: "Dad, today I want to steer!" Lolo splashed yellow boots in the water on the boat floor. With all three in life jackets, the motorboat left the pier, putt, putt, putt. But Riri in her yellow hat held the tiller with both hands.
"I want to hold it just once too!" Lolo reached out. Dad the fisherman placed his big hand over the handle. "Then take turns holding it." The boat moved ahead.
But Riri did not let go. "Wait, it is not straight yet." She turned a little, then a little more, narrowing her eyes. Beside her, Lolo could only stamp impatiently.

Seagulls passed, then the lighthouse, but the handle stayed with Riri. "Now it really is straight. Just one more!" She gripped it again. Lolo rested their chin on the side, letting both arms hang outside.
Dad came beside the tiller and placed a hand on Riri's. "Riri, how might Lolo feel, waiting like that all the time?" She looked up. "...I think I would stamp my feet too."
Dad pointed at waves meeting the bow. "Can you count how many waves come?" Riri counted on her fingers. Splash, splash—the boat crossed them. "Ten! ...Oh? Ten already?"
"At ten, we change hands on the handle." Dad smiled. Riri's eyes sparkled. "Oh, ten waves, then your turn!" She took both hands off the tiller.
When Lolo held the handle, the boat went happily putt, putt, putt. This time, Riri counted waves. "One, two, three..." Lolo grinned. "Only ten, right? All right!"
The handle changed hands as waves passed one by one. "One, count ten waves! Two, at ten, pass the handle! Three, the one waiting counts!" Out at sea, the boat kept going putt, putt, putt.
After tying up the boat, Dad stroked both their heads with his wet hands. A little waiting gave each a turn. Lolo rested their chin on Riri's shoulder. "Ten waves, then your turn!"
